Nobody thinks about where their voice goes. I did, and it ruined every dictation app for me. So I built Wisprit. Dictation for the Mac that runs entirely on your machine. Hold a key, talk, let go, and your words appear wherever your cursor is, already cleaned up. Punctuation, capitals, the words the mic got wrong. No account, no subscription, and nothing you say ever leaves the laptop. The part people don't expect: your words show up in the field while you are still talking. Not after. Live, in the actual text box. Every other tool makes you wait and then pastes a block at the end. The other part I love: spell a word once and it remembers it forever. Say "Add Sharique to the invite, actually it's S H A R I Q U E" and it quietly fixes the name, drops the spelling instruction, and never gets it wrong again. Names, jargon, whatever you use. It also never puts words in your mouth. Cleanup, yes — rewriting, never. Anything it isn't certain about comes back exactly as you said it. I'd rather ship an app that does nothing than one that says something I didn't. Free, local, and mine. Turns out the whole thing fits on the chip that's already in your Mac.

Today is extra special. I just ended my 12-week internship at Salesforce with an incredible experience. And today also marks exactly two years since I packed my two bags from Ghana to pursue higher education at Grambling State University . If anyone had told me three years ago the people I’d meet and what I’d accomplish within these past two years, I would have had my doubts. It’s been a crazy journey; one that began with a decision to risk it all. And that decision made all the difference.

Built and sold 2 products at hackathons last weekend, and won at both. Turns out selling during the event is a great way to differentiate yourself and prove your product. First one: an SEO/AEO agent that does more than just providing feedback, it continuously updates and optimizes how well your site ranks, through both internal (providing diffs) and external (calling blog sites to get citations) actions. Sold it to one of the sponsors during the hackathon. Second one: a browser extension agent that makes buying things harder instead of easier. When you go to buy something, it decides whether the purchase is silly. If it is, you have to argue your case, while it throws cheaper alternatives at you and reminds you of the similar junk you bought last month and regretted. If you win, it lets you buy. If not, it blocks you from spending. Sold 6-month subscriptions to 6 other people during the hackathon. Secret third win?? Four days of SF magic. I landed Monday knowing almost nobody. Then: a hackathon, a demo night, another hackathon, a win. Every room led to another room. One of those rooms turned out to float. Congrats to the whole Bland team. Phone calls, the least glamorous channel in tech, just became a Series C story. It hit different for me too. Donna, my hackathon winner from two days ago, runs on AI phone calls between food banks and donors. Watching a team take that same primitive from demo to Series C is the whole roadmap in one night. Pulled up with Kartikey Pandey and Kanika Gupta . Met Matthew Eernisse , Imisha Juneja , and builders from half the AI companies in the city. Nobody asked for a deck. This city rewards showing up. 9 days left. Follow along.

Most teams ship a demo in 24 hours. We shipped a full research paper — confidence intervals on every claim, an outside model checking our work, and three documented failures. And it won. This weekend Parth Kshirsagar and I built ReCompress and took 1st at the University of California, Berkeley 's AI Hackathon — The Token Company (YC W26) 's compression challenge ($11.7M raised, judging us on the exact problem they raise money to solve). The thesis: everyone compresses prompts by deleting low-value tokens. Fast — but blind. Deletion can't read your question, and it can't rewrite. So we built a compressor that does both, then distilled it into a 1.5B model small enough to run on the edge. The result: → 0.704 F1 vs the production system's 0.452 — a 56% jump → at ~8.5× fewer tokens out (48 vs 409) → and it still runs offline on a 1.5B model. We didn't trade the edge to get the accuracy. But the number isn't the flex. The rigor behind it is. We named our 5 distillation runs instead of calling them v1–v5: Spark (too little data — failed). Bonfire (overfit — failed). Hearth (the winner). Oracle + Oracle-Lite (a "smarter" idea that lost — twice). Three failures. All in the paper. 9 hours of training on a Modal H100 to get there — 45+ minutes a run, over and over, until Hearth landed. Then we tried to break our own win. Our teacher and solver were both DeepSeek — so of course a skeptic says "same model family, rigged result." So we re-ran the whole eval with Claude Sonnet, a totally different model, as the judge. The gap held: +0.288 vs +0.285. Not rigged. The whole thing cost $27 in free credits. One weekend. One paper that tried to disprove itself and couldn't. Most hackathon teams hide their failures. We made them the paper. Paper & code in the comments. Tell me where we're still wrong. 👇
